name: Power-assisted liposuction (PAL)

lead: Power-assisted liposuction uses a cannula driven by a motor so it vibrates as it moves through fat. People use it to remove stubborn fat for a leaner, smoother contour, and it is also described for male chest reduction and fat harvesting.

The motorized handpiece moves the cannula rapidly back and forth, which proponents say lowers the surgeon's effort and eases passage through fat. It is typically paired with tumescent anesthetic solution. Published work is mostly surgeons describing their technique, and few randomized trials compare it with conventional liposuction.

paras: It is a surgical operation performed by a surgeon, followed by compression garments and several weeks of swelling that settles. The final contour shows after healing.

It shares liposuction risks reported in the literature, including pain, bruising, contour irregularities, infection, bleeding and clots, with rare deaths. Risk is reported to increase with the volume removed.

angle.text: PAL is a motorized liposuction variant used to remove stubborn fat in a smooth, controlled way. A vibrating cannula takes out local fat deposits for a leaner contour once healed. Few trials compare it directly with conventional liposuction.

lead: Power-assisted liposuction (PAL) is a variant of suction lipectomy in which the cannula is driven by a motor so that it vibrates or reciprocates rapidly while the surgeon moves it through subcutaneous fat. It is one of several liposuction techniques, alongside tumescent, ultrasound-assisted, laser-assisted and water-jet-assisted methods.[1]

Proponents of the technique say the mechanical motion lets surgeons remove fat with less manual effort, and it has been described in published surgical reports for body contouring, superficial liposuction, gynecomastia in men and fat harvesting for grafting.[1][2][3] In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned mainly as a body-contouring option within the broader category of liposuction.

Published evidence consists mostly of surgeons' case series and small comparative studies; few randomized trials compare PAL with conventional suction-assisted liposuction, and the procedure is a surgical operation with the same general risk categories as other forms of liposuction.[1][4]
infobox: Local, regional or general, depending on extent

paras: In conventional liposuction a surgeon manually pushes and pulls a hollow cannula connected to suction through the fat layer. In power-assisted liposuction the cannula is attached to a handpiece that moves it back and forth at high frequency, a design that its advocates say reduces surgeon fatigue and speeds fat removal.[1] The procedure is usually combined with tumescent infiltration of local anesthetic solution.[1]

Reports describe PAL used with a pull-through approach to treat gynecomastia in men, in which fat and glandular tissue are removed through small incisions.[3] Surgeons have also used powered or vibrating cannulas to harvest fat for transfer, including large-volume gluteal fat grafting.[4][5]

Superficial liposuction, which works in the fat layer close to the skin to improve contour, has its own published complication analysis covering 2,398 cases, although that review concerns superficial technique in general rather than power assistance specifically.[2]

Complications described for liposuction in general include pain, bruising, swelling, contour irregularities, altered sensation, infection, bleeding, blood clots and, rarely, death, according to summaries of the literature.[1] A US survey of liposuction practice published in 2011 documented trends in how the procedure is performed and by whom.[6] Risk is reported to rise with the volume removed.[1]

A prospective randomized trial published in 2007 compared postoperative pain after power water-assisted and traditional liposuction.[7] A 2014 laboratory study compared adipose-derived stem cells obtained by power-assisted and manual aspiration in terms of viability and ability to differentiate into fat cells.[8] A registered 2026 trial (NCT07820397) is comparing adipose tissue viability after different liposuction approaches within the same patients.[9] A registered study of harmonic vibration liposuction (NCT07889427) enrolled 13 participants.[10] Most other published work is descriptive surgical technique reports.[3][4]

lore.intro: Power-assisted liposuction appears in forum discussions of body-contouring surgery, usually as one named option among liposuction technologies rather than as a looksmaxxing topic in its own right.

claims.claim: A vibrating cannula gives smoother, more precise fat removal than manual liposuction
